newsitem.title: UK: Top firms warn Britain on shunning single currency.
newsitem.headline: Top firms warn Britain on shunning single currency.

text.p: A group of 15 top British companies warned on Thursday of the dangers of Britain shunning a single European currency.

The industrialists joined the debate over Britain's role in a single European currency as pressure grows on prime minister John Major from some sections within the ruling Conservative party to rule out British involvement.
They voiced their concerns in a letter to the Financial Times newspaper, a move the paper said followed talks at the Confederation of British Industry.

"We believe that a self-imposed exclusion from negotiations over Emu (European Monetary Union) would be deeply damaging," Allied Domecq chief executive Tony Hales said in a letter to the editor of the Financial Times on behalf of 14 other firms.
The letter pointed out the companies were involved in European trade generating "billions of dollars of export business and creates tens of thousands of jobs (in Britain)".
Earlier this week a top official in the City of London warned that jobs were at risk in the capital if Britain did not join France and Germany in a single currency.

And a report by an independent think-tank on Monday said Britain's lack of preparation for the single European currency could cost up to 20,000 jobs in industry and the City of London's financial district.

The letter was signed by the chief executive or chairman of B.A.T Industries, British Aerospace, British Petroleum, BUPA, Burson-Marsteller/Europe, Coopers & Lybrand, Glaxo Wellcome, Guinness, Northern Foods, Rentokil, Shell Transport and Trading, Unigate, Unilever and Vauxhall Motors.
"Many aspects of monetary union remain to be resolved. Leaving an empty chair at the table would mean that British interests would be unrepresented as crucial decisions were taken," it added.
It said such a gesture "could leave British businesses at a competitive disadvantage for years to come".
Continued participation in the preparation for a single currency would ensure Britain could protect its own interests as well as reassuring inward investors, the industrialists said.
Such investors would "perhaps rightly, interpret any decision to rule out membership as the first act in a process of disengagement from one of the largest markets in the world".
The Financial Times said there was pressure on Major to rule out British participation in monetary union, either at the start date of 1999 or in the five-year life of the next parliament.

It said the Treasury had been sent a copy of the letter, adding that only about half of the businessmen approached had agreed to sign the letter, with large clearing banks among those unwilling to add their names.
